title: Chapter 24: Virtual Environments and Packages
video_title: Python Chapter 24: Virtual Environments and Packages
summary: Asha gives her weather board its own Python with venv, installs packages with python -m pip, and records exact versions in requirements.txt. She learns to check every package name before installing, and measures look-alike names with difflib. Then she adds a package with an AI assistant at all six stages, catching a wrong cutoff, a dangerous install command and a suggestion to skip the virtual environment.

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: A **package** is code from someone else that you install, such as `requests`.
Most packages live on **PyPI**, at pypi.org. Anyone can publish there.
A name one letter away from a famous package can hide harmful code.
The cafe laptop and the home laptop must run the board the same way.

segments.say: Asha needs requests for live weather, and tabulate for a neat table. They are packages: code that other people shared. Most live on PyPI, at pypi dot org.
Anyone can publish there, so a look-alike name can hide harmful code. And her board must run the same way on two laptops.

scenes.title: The idea: one toolbox per project
scenes.direction: Teach the diagram, the toolbox analogy and where it stops, then the words table. Quiz, then a breather.

visual.heading: A virtual environment
visual.label: The idea
body: A **virtual environment** is a folder with its own Python and packages, for one project.
visual.pre:
Without a virtual environment      With one per project
  ---------------------------        ------------------------------
  Computer Python                    weather_board/
    requests 2.31                      .venv/  requests, tabulate
    tabulate                         quiz_app/
    every project's packages           .venv/  pytest

segments.say: Here is the big idea. A virtual environment is a folder that holds its own Python and its own packages, for one project.
Without one, every project's packages get mixed together in the computer's Python.

visual.heading: Like a toolbox for each project
visual.label: Analogy
items: The weather board's tools never mix with the quiz app's tools.
Where it stops working: you cannot carry the toolbox to another computer.
On a new computer, you build a new one from a list.

segments.say: Think of a separate toolbox for each project. The weather board's tools never get mixed up with the quiz app's tools.
The comparison stops working at one point. A virtual environment is built for one computer. You cannot carry it to another one.
On a new computer, you build a new one, from a list of what the project needs.

visual.heading: Five words for this chapter
visual.label: The idea
rows: Code from someone else that you install
The Python Package Index at pypi.org
The tool that installs packages from PyPI
A project folder, `.venv`, with its own Python and packages

segments.say: Pip is the tool that installs packages from PyPI.
The virtual environment is usually a folder called dot v e n v.
And a pinned version names one exact version, with two equals signs. A list of them is called requirements dot t x t.

scenes.title: Steps 1 and 2: Create and activate
scenes.direction: Create command per system, what is inside, activate per system, the prompt and the sys.prefix check. Ask about a new terminal.

visual.heading: Step 1: Create a virtual environment
visual.label: Build it
columns: Type this in the project folder

segments.say: Step 1. Asha opens a terminal in her project folder. She runs v e n v, the standard module that makes virtual environments, and names the folder dot v e n v.
On Windows, she types p y, dash m, v e n v, dot v e n v.
On macOS and Linux, python3, dash m, v e n v, dot v e n v. Nothing prints, but a new folder appears, with its own python and pip.
Step 2. Activating tells this terminal to use the Python inside dot v e n v.
On Windows, dot v e n v, backslash, Scripts, backslash, activate.
In PowerShell, the script ends in dot p s 1. The lesson shows what to do if PowerShell refuses it.
On macOS and Linux, source, dot v e n v, slash, bin, slash, activate.
To leave it, type deactivate. And one rule: activate it again every time you open a new terminal.

visual.heading: Am I inside?
visual.label: Build it
visual.pre:
$ source .venv/bin/activate
  (.venv) $ python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)"
  True

segments.say: Now the prompt starts with dot v e n v in brackets. Asha checks it with one line of Python.
Sys dot prefix is the folder of the Python that is running. Sys dot base prefix is the computer's own Python. They differ only inside a virtual environment, so this prints True.
The next morning, Asha opens a new terminal, and types python straight away.

ask.question: In that new terminal, which Python runs: the one in `.venv`, or the computer's own?

after.say: The computer's own Python. A new terminal starts outside, so she must activate dot v e n v again. The prompt tells her: no dot v e n v in brackets, not inside.

scenes.title: Steps 3 and 4: Install, record, reinstall
scenes.direction: Install and list, freeze and install -r, then read the pinned file with ex01 and predict line 10.

visual.heading: Step 3: Install a package
visual.label: Build it
body: `python -m` makes pip install into the Python that is running.
visual.pre:
(.venv) $ python -m pip install tabulate
  (.venv) $ python -m pip list
  Package  Version
  -------- -------
  pip      26.2.2
  tabulate 0.9.0

segments.say: Step 3. With dot v e n v active, Asha installs tabulate. She types python, dash m, pip install, tabulate.
Python dash m makes sure pip installs into the Python she is running. Pip list then shows what is installed here. Your version numbers may differ.
In Chapter 19, you installed pytest once, with no virtual environment. From now on, each project's packages go inside its own dot v e n v.

visual.heading: Step 4: Record, then reinstall
visual.label: Build it
body: `pip freeze` prints every installed package as a pinned line.
visual.pre:
On the cafe laptop:
  (.venv) $ python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt

  On the computer at home, in a new .venv:
  (.venv) $ python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

segments.say: Step 4. Pip freeze prints every installed package as a pinned line. The greater than sign saves it into requirements dot t x t.
At home, Asha creates and activates a new dot v e n v. Then pip install, dash r, requirements dot t x t, installs exactly the same versions.

visual.heading: The board's requirements file
visual.label: Build it
body: The versions here are examples. Check pypi.org for the version you want.
visual.pre:
requirements.txt
  # Packages for the weather board
  requests==2.32.3
  tabulate==0.9.0

segments.say: Here is the board's file. The hash sign line is a comment. Each other line pins one package.
Asha's program reads that file. Lines 4 and 5 read the text, and line 6 goes through it.
Lines 8 and 9 skip empty lines and comments.
Line 10 splits each line at the two equals signs, so name gets the package, and version gets the number.
Line 11 prints the name in ten spaces, then the version.

ask.question: What does line 11 print for each package?

after.say: Requests and 2.32.3, then tabulate and 0.9.0. The comment line never reaches line 11.

scenes.title: Step 5: Pinned or not?
scenes.direction: Teach what makes a line pinned, then predict ex02, then a quiz and a breather.

segments.say: Step 5. A line without two equals signs lets pip choose the version. That version can change next month.
Greater than, equals, 8 means 8 or newer. That is not exact either.
Line 4 calls a line pinned only if it contains two equals signs together.

ask.question: Which of the three lines does this program call pinned?

after.say: Only the first: requests, pinned at 2.32.3. Tabulate has no version, and pytest only says 8 or newer.
Those two lines could install different code on Asha's two laptops.

visual.question: Which line installs exactly the same version on every computer?
visual.explain: Two equals signs pin one exact version.

segments.say: Quick check. Which line installs exactly the same version on every computer?

after.say: D. Two equals signs pin one exact version. Look closely at C. It has only one.

items: Create `.venv`, then activate it.
Install with `python -m pip`.
Pin exact versions with `==`.

segments.say: Breather. Asha's board now has its own toolbox, and a list of exact versions. Next, the most important habit: checking a name first.

scenes.title: Step 6: Check a name first
scenes.direction: The four checks on a PyPI page, then difflib scores. Speak the score, then ask what line 7 prints.

visual.heading: Step 6: Four checks before you install
visual.label: Build it
columns: What to look for on pypi.org
rows: Every letter matches. Capital letters do not count.
Links to the source code and documentation
How long it has existed, and the last update
Who publishes it, and the same names in the documentation

segments.say: Step 6. Before Asha installs a package, she opens its page on pypi dot org, and makes four checks.
One. The exact name: every letter must match. PyPI ignores capital letters, so Requests with a capital R is the same package.
Two, links to its code and documentation.
Three, its release history.
Four, who publishes it.
A name one or two letters away from a famous one is a warning sign. People publish look-alike names on purpose, hoping for a spelling mistake.
The standard module diff lib measures how alike two names are. Its score goes from 0, nothing alike, to 1, the same.
Line 5 compares reqeusts with requests. Its first argument, None, means no characters are ignored. Even with two letters swapped, line 6 prints a score of 0.875.
Line 7 uses get close matches. It returns a list of the trusted names whose score is at least the cutoff, here 0.8.

after.say: Line 7 prints a list with requests, because 0.875 is at least 0.8.
Line 8 prints an empty list. Num py is not like any trusted name.

scenes.title: See the outcome: Asha's list check
scenes.direction: Walk the program in two excerpts, ask which lines of the draft are reported, then reveal. Hand over to the AI story.

segments.say: Back to the mission. Line 5 is the trusted list, lines 6 and 7 read the draft, and line 8 counts problems.
Line 13 takes the name before the two equals signs, in small letters.
Lines 14 to 16 report a line with no pin, and count it.
Line 17 catches a pinned name that is not on the trusted list.
Line 18 finds the closest trusted names. Line 19 takes the first one, with the if else from Chapter 14, in case nothing is close.
Lines 20 and 21 report it and count it. Any other line is OK, and line 24 prints the total.

scenes.title: Work with AI: adding a package safely
scenes.direction: Six stages on adding a package safely with name_check(). Plan misses the name check. Generate's cutoff misses reqeusts. Test fails two cases, then all pass. Debug: the AI says install the look-alike. Improve: sudo is rejected.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: check every name
visual.label: Before you start
items: An AI can name a package that does not exist, or one with a spelling mistake.
Attackers can publish packages with exactly those names.
Never install a name from a chat before you check it.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill: check every package an AI suggests. It can name a package that does not exist, and attackers can publish exactly those names.
So never install a name from a chat before you check it. And never paste keys, passwords or private data.

messages.text: My weather board needs a package to fetch live weather. Do not write code yet. List the steps to add a package to my project safely.

1. Create and activate a virtual environment.
2. Install requests with python -m pip.
3. Test the board.
4. Record the version with pip freeze in requirements.txt.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha asks for the steps to add a package to her project safely. No code yet.
Four good steps. But one is missing: check the name and its page on pypi dot org, before installing. Asha adds it as step 2.

messages.text: I wrote this name check myself. Do not rewrite it. What does it return for reqeusts?
It returns "unknown: check pypi.org". Only exact names in TRUSTED return "trusted".
I ran it. That is right:

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha writes her own name check first. It only knows exact names.
The AI says reqeusts gives unknown. She runs it: right. But her version cannot warn about look-alikes.

messages.text: Write a version that also warns when a name looks like a trusted name. Use difflib. What does it return for reqeusts?
Here it is. For reqeusts, it returns "look-alike of requests".

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha asks for a version that warns about look-alike names, using diff lib.
The AI says reqeusts will return: look-alike of requests.
Look at line 10. The cutoff is 0.9. Remember the score of reqeusts from step 6.

ask.question: The AI says line 16 prints `look-alike of requests`. Is it right?

after.say: No. Reqeusts scores only 0.875, below the cutoff of 0.9. So line 13 says unknown.

visual.heading: Test: four cases on the AI's code

messages.text: My four cases: requests is trusted. reqeusts is a look-alike of requests. Requests is trusted. numpy is unknown. I will run them on your code.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha writes four cases with the exact result she expects, including Requests with a capital R.
The AI says all four will pass.

visual.heading: Four cases, on the AI's version

segments.say: Lines 16 to 19 hold the four cases. Line 23 prints pass or fail for each.
Remember: PyPI ignores capital letters. Look at line 8.

ask.question: Which of the four cases fail?

after.say: Two fail. Reqeusts, because of the cutoff. And Requests, because line 8 compares the exact text, with its capital R.

visual.heading: Test: the cause, then the fix

messages.text: Two cases fail: reqeusts and Requests. Explain the cause of each, then fix them.

reqeusts scores 0.875, below my cutoff of 0.9. Use 0.8.
Requests has a capital R. Change the name to small letters with lower() first.

segments.say: Asha shows the AI the two failures, and asks for the cause of each first.
The AI lowers the cutoff to 0.8, and changes the name to small letters before comparing.
Line 8 lowers the name, and line 11 uses 0.8. She runs all four cases again. All four pass.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: My weather script stopped with this error. Explain the cause first.

The package is not installed. Run this command:
python -m pip install reqeusts

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Asha copies an import line from a chat into her weather script. It stops with a module not found error. She asks for the cause first.
The AI says the package is not installed, and gives her the install command for reqeusts.

ask.question: Should Asha run the command the AI gave her?

after.say: No. Not before she checks the name. It is the same look-alike from her draft.

segments.say: She runs her name check. Reqeusts: look-alike of requests.
So the real problem is a spelling mistake in her import line, not a missing package. She fixes it to requests, and installs requests inside her virtual environment.
The look-alike could have run someone else's code on the cafe laptop.

visual.heading: Her four cases, one more run

segments.say: She runs her four cases again on the name check. All four still pass.

messages.text: My setup works. Suggest at most two improvements, each with one reason.

1. Remove spaces with strip(). A name copied from a chat can carry spaces.
2. Skip the virtual environment. Install with sudo, and add --break-system-packages if pip refuses.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Her setup works. Asha asks for at most two improvements.
One. Remove spaces with strip, because a name copied from a chat can carry spaces. That is useful.

Two. Skip the virtual environment, and force the install with break system packages. That forces pip to change the computer's own Python, which other programs need. It breaks this chapter's first rule, so Asha says no.

visual.heading: Five cases, after the strip change

segments.say: She keeps suggestion one. Line 8 now strips spaces, and line 21 adds a fifth case: requests, with spaces around it. She runs every case again. All five pass.

visual.question: An AI says: install this package to fix the error. What do you do first?
options: Check the exact name and its pypi.org page
visual.explain: Check the name and its page before you install anything.

segments.say: Quick check. An AI says: install this package to fix the error. What do you do first?

after.say: B. Check the exact name and its page on pypi dot org. Then decide.

items: Plan, write, generate, test, debug, improve.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 calls back to activating. Mistake 2 is a spot-it on the pin. Mistakes 3 and 4 are messages and habits.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: the environment is not active

segments.say: Mistake 1. Asha installs a package in her virtual environment, opens a new terminal, and runs her board. Here, weather tables stands for that package. It stops with a module not found error.
Check the prompt first. With no dot v e n v in brackets, the terminal uses the computer's Python, where the package is not installed. Activate, then run again.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: Mistake 2. Remember the pinned lines from step 5.

ask.question: What is wrong with the pin on line 2?

after.say: It has only one equals sign. So line 3 finds no two equals signs to split at, and gets only one part.
after.heading: Mistake 2: one equals sign in a pin

after.say: Not enough values to unpack means: two names are waiting, but only one value arrived. Write two equals signs. Pip refuses the single one too.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: installing into the computer's Python
visual.label: Common mistakes
body: Some systems refuse a plain `pip install` outside a virtual environment.

segments.say: Mistake 3. Some systems refuse a plain pip install outside a virtual environment. Do not force it, as the AI suggested. Activate a virtual environment, and install there.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: copying the .venv folder
visual.label: Common mistakes
items: A virtual environment holds paths for one computer.
Copied to another computer or folder, it may stop working.
Share `requirements.txt` instead, and build a new `.venv` on each computer.

segments.say: Mistake 4. A virtual environment holds paths for one computer. Copied to another computer or folder, it may stop working.
So never share dot v e n v. Share requirements dot t x t, and build a new environment on each computer.

items: No `(.venv)` in the prompt: activate first.
Pins need two equals signs.
Share `requirements.txt`, never `.venv`.

scenes.title: Recap
scenes.direction: Each recap point appears as it is spoken, then a final quick check, then the badge.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: A virtual environment is a project folder, `.venv`, with its own Python and packages.
Look for `(.venv)` in the prompt before you install anything.
`python -m pip install` adds a package. `pip list` shows what is installed.
`requirements.txt` pins versions with `==`. `pip install -r` installs the same versions.
Check every name on pypi.org. A look-alike name is a warning sign.
Never install a name from an AI before you check it.

segments.say: A virtual environment is a project folder with its own Python and packages.
Look for dot v e n v in the prompt, then install with python dash m pip.
Requirements dot t x t pins exact versions for every computer.
And check every name before you install it, especially a name from an AI.

visual.question: Which command records the exact versions in the active environment?
visual.explain: `pip freeze` prints pinned lines, and `>` saves them in a file.

segments.say: One last check. Which command records the exact versions in the active environment, in a file?

after.say: A. Pip freeze prints pinned lines, and the greater than sign saves them in requirements dot t x t. Pip list only shows them.
